newsitem.title: USA: Dollar to hit 130 yen, 1.80 marks in 1997-Merrill.
newsitem.headline: Dollar to hit 130 yen, 1.80 marks in 1997-Merrill.

text.p: Favorable interest rate differentials will propel the dollar higher to 130 yen and 1.80 marks in late 1997, according to a report released by Merrill Lynch and Co.

The report, issued on Wednesday by senior international economist John Praveen and chief economist Donald Straszheim, cites the inability of Germany and Japan to raise interest rates and the virtual certainty that official U.S. rates will not go lower in 1997.
"This move is precluded since it would exacerbate U.S. inflation risks while short-circuiting the fragile recoveries in Europe and Japan," the report said.
While officials in some Group of Seven nations have expressed a desire to halt the dollar's advance, they have only limited tools for achieving that outcome, the economists said.
"The G7 is restricted to marginally effective verbal support and dollar-selling intervention in currency markets," the report said.
However, fears that the weak mark will boost German inflation present an argument in favor of higher German interest rates, Merrill noted.

According to Merrill's top German economist, the Bundesbank was confident in early January that inflation would stay below 2.0 percent through 1999, allowing steady interest rates leading up to European Economic and Monetary Union.
But since then the dollar has continued to assault the mark, raising the chances of higher German rates, Merrill said.
"The relentless plunge in the deutschemark, which has lost 15 pfennings since the start of 1997, has raised the risk that Buba may be forced to act much earlier," the report said.
